clue.text: See doctor at four, fit and roadworthy

parts.note: DR is the standard abbreviation for doctor
four in Roman numerals
fit to do something is able to do it

explanation.surface: A patient is told to see the doctor at four o'clock to be declared fit, like a car passing its inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See doctor at four' reads like an appointment, but the time is a Roman numeral placed next to the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A vehicle that is roadworthy is in a safe condition to be driven on public highways.

clue.text: Female chief cried about lock of hair

indicators.note: about suggests moving around, so these letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a tress is a long lock of hair

explanation.surface: A woman boss wept over a curl of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A directress is the old feminine form for a woman who directs or leads an organisation.

clue.text: More than one aim under canvas is to hold on

parts.note: under canvas means camping, in a tent

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A camper has several goals, one being to hang on in the tent.
explanation.definitionFit: Intentions are plans or purposes, the plural of what someone aims to achieve.

clue.text: Lewis Carroll's girl is caught in a lie

indicators.note: something in another sits inside it

parts.note: taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: The heroine of Wonderland is found out telling an untruth.
explanation.walkthrough: On a cricket scorecard, c stands for caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice is the heroine of Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass.

clue.text: Burning to pick up the girl and cohabit

parts.note: live coals are burning ones
to pick up is to get, and the girl is her

explanation.surface: A man is eager to collect his girlfriend and move in with her.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who cohabit share a home as partners without being married.

clue.text: US spacecraft keeps its head in a ring

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so the head goes between the outer pieces

parts.note: taken as written
a ring is round like the letter O
poll is an old word for the head, as in poll tax

explanation.surface: A spacecraft stays steady, keeping its nose centred within a ring, as on a docking manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: A and O join first, then the old word for head goes in between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was the NASA programme whose craft carried astronauts to the Moon between 1968 and 1972.

clue.text: Bloodsucking as it appears in Capri quaintly

indicators.note: done quaintly means in an odd, unusual way, so these letters are set in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mosquitoes bite on the charming Italian island of Capri.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasitic creature lives off a host, as leeches and ticks feed on blood.

clue.text: Culinary vegetable, sleek if top not cut off

indicators.note: the answer would be the given word had its first letter not been lopped, so that letter is gone

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook notes that a vegetable looks glossy when its top is left on.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as: the vegetable would be sleek if its top letter had not been cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: The leek is an onion relative used in soups and stews, a staple kitchen vegetable.

clue.text: Headless women acting as a warning

indicators.note: without a head means the first letter of the next word is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ghostly women without heads appear as a sign of doom.
explanation.definitionFit: An omen is a sign foretelling something, often taken as a warning of trouble ahead.

clue.text: Recapture and revere it like this

indicators.note: the words are to be put into the form shown by the definition, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: the eight letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to win something back and then treat it with deep respect.
explanation.definitionFit: To recapture something is to get it back again, which is what retrieving a lost thing means.

clue.text: Hear ornamental band become rigid

indicators.note: we are told to listen, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a frieze is a decorative band along the top of a wall

explanation.surface: A visitor admires a decorative band in a building and stiffens on the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that freezes turns solid, and a person who freezes stops moving, stiff with fear or cold.

clue.text: Wearied folk and unlucky savers might do

definitions.note: people; the answer is what they might do
definitions.meaning: first meaning: bored people stop caring about something

definitions.note: people; the answer is what they might do
definitions.meaning: second meaning: savers who are unlucky forfeit the return on their deposits

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works once as boredom and once as a literal loss of money earned by savings.
explanation.definitionFit: Bored people stop paying attention, and savers whose bank fails forfeit the money their deposits earned.

clue.text: Argumentative but happy with later promises

parts.note: content means satisfied, pleased
IOUs are written promises to pay back later

explanation.surface: A quarrelsome person is cheerful as long as they are owed a few promises.
explanation.walkthrough: An IOU ('I owe you') is a note acknowledging a debt to be settled later.
explanation.definitionFit: A contentious person or issue causes disputes and quarrels, so it is likely to provoke argument.

clue.text: Kicked around a referee without shoes

indicators.note: one word goes around another, enclosing it

parts.note: to boot something is to kick it
taken as written
ref is the short form of referee

explanation.surface: Players kick out at a match official, without any boots on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kicked around' reads as a phrase meaning mistreated, but 'around' tells the kick to wrap the official.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone barefooted walks with bare feet, wearing no shoes or socks.

clue.text: Young French woman: "Lilo seemed wobbly"

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady and out of order, so these letters are moved around

parts.note: the letters of these two words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A young Frenchwoman remarks that the inflatable airbed seemed unsteady.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lilo is a British brand of inflatable airbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoiselle is French for a young unmarried lady, borrowed into English.

clue.text: Former BBC chief upset her with it

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A retired head of the BBC is annoyed with a woman over something.
explanation.definitionFit: John Reith was the founding Director-General of the British Broadcasting Corporation in the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Fifty per cent on top of old coin

parts.note: fifty per cent is one half
the crown is the top of the head or of a hill

explanation.surface: Half of something sits above an antique coin, like a stack of change.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' puts the first piece above the second. The half-crown was a British coin worth two shillings and sixpence, withdrawn in 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: The half-crown was a pre-decimal British silver coin, now out of circulation.

clue.text: Hamlet's very large dog?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Shakespeare's prince of Denmark, a famous person from that country
second meaning: a giant breed of hound

explanation.surface: It sounds like asking about the Danish prince's enormous pet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', not possession; the question mark flags the playful reading of Hamlet as a notable native of Denmark.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is a celebrated prince of Denmark, and the same phrase names the huge breed of dog.

clue.text: Only child with vest on

parts.note: a singlet is a sleeveless vest
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lone youngster runs about with nothing but a vest on.
explanation.walkthrough: In British use a vest is an undershirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A child with no brothers or sisters is called a singleton, a word for anything existing alone.

clue.text: My belief is that wine is absorbed in company

indicators.note: something absorbed in another is taken inside it, so the drink goes within the firm

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
red is a colour of wine

explanation.surface: Someone declares their creed: wine is best drunk in good company.
explanation.definitionFit: Credo is Latin for 'I believe' and names a personal creed or statement of principles.

clue.text: I'm oversure of my own ability, having smart wooden shoes

definitions.text: I'm oversure of my own ability
definitions.note: the clue gives a sentence a know-all might say; the answer is the noun naming such a person

parts.note: smart means bright, quick-witted
clogs are shoes with wooden soles

explanation.surface: A boaster brags about their talents while showing off fashionable wooden footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Clever clogs is British slang for a smart aleck; 'smart' here is intelligence, not style.
explanation.definitionFit: A clever clogs is an informal name for a show-off who thinks they know best.

clue.text: Pincer-like claw displayed by Rachel acting

indicators.note: something displayed by these words is on show within them, spanning the gap

parts.note: the run of letters across the end of the name and start of the next word

explanation.surface: An actress named Rachel mimes a crab's grip on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A chela is the zoological term for the pincer of a crab, lobster or scorpion.

clue.text: Leading lady accommodates second sailor

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
tar is old slang for a sailor

explanation.surface: An actress in the main role makes room for a second seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: The star of a show is its principal performer, the one who takes the lead role.

clue.text: Starting pistols, for example, hung up in pub's small room

indicators.note: in a down entry, hung up means raised from bottom to top, so the word reads upward

parts.note: starting pistols are a kind of firearm

explanation.surface: Starter's pistols are hung on the wall of a cosy back room in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A snug is a small private bar room in a British pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The snug is a small, cosy side room in a traditional British public house.

clue.text: Money attracts marijuana, which is worthless

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A warning that cash draws in drugs, which have no value.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinpot describes something shabby, inferior or of little importance, like a tinpot dictator.

clue.text: Desmond breaks up a petal, which is base

indicators.note: something that breaks up another splits it apart and sits in the gap

parts.note: taken as written
Des is the short form of the name Desmond

explanation.surface: A man named Desmond pulls a flower petal to pieces, which is a low act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like 'mean' after the destructive act, but it is the support a statue stands on.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base or support on which a column or statue stands.

clue.text: Administrator, for example, included in the rent

indicators.note: something included in another is placed inside it

parts.note: rent taken as written; 'the' is just part of the surface
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: An estate manager's fee, say, is counted in the rent tenants pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A regent administers a kingdom on behalf of a monarch who is too young, absent or unfit to rule.

clue.text: Spread legs wide to keep violin ''eld backwards

parts.note: a Strad is a Stradivarius violin

indicators.note: going backwards means this word is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: 'eld is 'held' with its H dropped, as in Cockney speech

explanation.surface: A cellist is told to sit with legs apart to keep the instrument held back.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe marks a dropped H, so only the three letters after it are used.
explanation.definitionFit: To straddle something is to sit or stand with one leg either side of it, legs apart.
